stem: After a failed `dbt build`, a developer wants to re-run only the nodes that genuinely need it, using `result:` selectors against the prior invocation's artifacts. Which TWO of the following are valid, documented `result` selectors?

option_texts.A: `result:error`, selecting resources that generated errors on the prior invocation
option_texts.B: `result:fail`, selecting tests that failed on the prior invocation
option_texts.C: `result:skipped`, selecting resources that were skipped because an upstream resource failed
option_texts.D: `result:pending`, selecting resources that have not been run yet in this invocation

drill_answer_short: result:error and result:fail are the documented result selectors
decision_hinge: The result method can be used to select resources based on their result status from a prior run. Run all models that generated errors on the prior invocation of dbt run using result:error. Run all tests that failed on the prior invocation of dbt test using result:fail.

plausible_options.C: wants to re-run only the nodes that genuinely need it, using `result:` selectors against the prior invocation's artifacts

eliminated_by.D: using `result:` selectors against the prior invocation's artifacts

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — skip propagation is real dbt behavior, but it is not exposed as a result: selector value
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — dbt's documented result method does not define a pending value

stem: A Slim CI pipeline only selects `state:modified` resources, but several of those modified models `ref()` parents that were never selected and don't yet exist in the CI schema. The team needs to know exactly what `--defer` does in this pipeline to prevent those refs from failing. What does `--defer` do?

option_texts.A: It resolves `ref()` calls for unselected, not-yet-built parents using a specified production state manifest instead
option_texts.B: It defers execution of failed models and their parents to a later retry, after the rest of the build finishes
option_texts.C: It postpones running any tests until every model in the selection has finished building
option_texts.D: It skips building any model that `--select` did not explicitly name, without touching how refs resolve

drill_answer_short: --defer resolves unselected, unbuilt parent refs using a specified state manifest
decision_hinge: When deferral conditions are met, dbt will resolve ref calls using the state manifest instead, but only if the node isn't among the selected nodes, and it doesn't exist in the database.

plausible_options.D: several of those modified models `ref()` parents that were never selected and don't yet exist in the CI schema

eliminated_by.B: The team needs to know exactly what `--defer` does in this pipeline to prevent those refs from failing
eliminated_by.C: The team needs to know exactly what `--defer` does in this pipeline to prevent those refs from failing

distractor_traps.B: T1: fabricated — --defer is about ref resolution for unselected nodes, not retry scheduling for failures
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — --defer does not reorder when tests run relative to models
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — --select already decides which nodes build; --defer changes only how refs to the rest resolve

stem: A Slim CI pipeline must build only models whose SQL body genuinely changed compared to production, deliberately ignoring config-only changes like a renamed `tags` entry or a relocated schema. Which command is correct for this narrower scope?

option_texts.D: `dbt run --select state:modified --state ./prod-artifacts`, since the full modified criteria is always narrower than any subselector

drill_answer_short: state:modified.body selects only changes to the node body, such as model SQL
decision_hinge: state:modified.body: Changes to node body (e.g. model SQL, seed values). state:modified.configs: Changes to any node configs, excluding database/schema/alias/tags/meta.

plausible_options.B: deliberately ignoring config-only changes like a renamed `tags` entry or a relocated schema

eliminated_by.C: deliberately ignoring config-only changes like a renamed `tags` entry or a relocated schema

D.signal: must build only models whose SQL body genuinely changed compared to production
D.requires_fact: state:modified subselectors each include a subset of the full modified criteria; the full state:modified is the broadest, not narrower than its own subselectors.

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — .configs tracks config changes, excluding tags and meta, which is the opposite scope from body changes
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — .relation tracks database/schema/alias changes, not the SQL body itself
distractor_traps.D: T4: breaks a stated fact — subselectors are narrower subsets of the full modified criteria, not the other way around

stem: A model's SQL stays byte-for-byte identical, but its `materialized` config changes from `view` to `table`. A reviewer needs to know which of the two `state:modified` subselectors, `.body` or `.configs`, actually flags this specific change. Which one does, and why?

option_texts.A: `.configs`, because it tracks config edits, and `.body` only tracks the node's SQL or seed values
option_texts.B: `.body`, because any functional change to how a model builds counts as a body change
option_texts.C: Both subselectors flag it, since a materialization config change ultimately alters the node's compiled configs too
option_texts.D: Neither subselector flags it, since only a full `state:modified` catches any node configs change

drill_answer_short: .configs tracks config changes like materialized; .body only tracks the SQL or seed values themselves
decision_hinge: state:modified.body: Changes to node body (e.g. model SQL, seed values). state:modified.configs: Changes to any node configs, excluding database/schema/alias/tags/meta.

plausible_options.B: A model's SQL stays byte-for-byte identical, but its `materialized` config changes

eliminated_by.C: A model's SQL stays byte-for-byte identical, but its `materialized` config changes
eliminated_by.D: A model's SQL stays byte-for-byte identical, but its `materialized` config changes

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — .body is specifically about node body, which the stem says stayed byte-for-byte identical
distractor_traps.C: T4: breaks a stated fact — the stem says the SQL itself is unchanged, so the body subselector does not fire
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — the .configs subselector is specifically designed to catch exactly this kind of config change

stem: A `unique` test is declared on an incremental model's primary key column. The team needs to know exactly which rows that test query evaluates when `dbt test` runs: only the rows inserted or merged during the most recent incremental run, or something broader. What does the test actually evaluate?

option_texts.A: The model's entire current relation in the warehouse, since a generic test resolves `{{ model }}` to the full existing table, not a batch of recent rows
option_texts.B: Only the rows affected by the most recent incremental run, since dbt tracks which rows were just inserted or merged
option_texts.C: Only the rows that existed before the incremental model's very first run
option_texts.D: No rows at all, since data tests cannot run against incremental models

drill_answer_short: A data test queries the model's full current relation, not just the latest incremental batch
decision_hinge: A generic data test is defined in a test block with a parameterized query, templating model and column_name. The ref() function returns a Relation for a model, pointing at its current database object.

plausible_options.B: only the rows inserted or merged during the most recent incremental run, or something broader

eliminated_by.C: The team needs to know exactly which rows that test query evaluates when `dbt test` runs
eliminated_by.D: The team needs to know exactly which rows that test query evaluates when `dbt test` runs

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — dbt does not scope a generic test query to only the most recently changed rows
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — a test query has no documented mechanism to isolate pre-first-run rows specifically
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — data tests fully support incremental models, the same as any other materialization

stem: A CI/CD pipeline uses `dbt build --select state:modified+ result:error+ --defer --state ./prod-artifacts --target ci`. The team needs to know what the plain space between `state:modified+` and `result:error+` actually means for how these two selector expressions combine. What does the space mean here?

option_texts.A: A union: any resource matching either `state:modified+` or `result:error+` is selected
option_texts.B: An intersection: a resource must match both `state:modified+` and `result:error+` to be selected
option_texts.C: Exclusion: resources matching `result:error+` are removed from the `state:modified+` selection
option_texts.D: Sequencing: `state:modified+` runs first, then `result:error+` runs as a separate, later step

drill_answer_short: A space between selector expressions is a union (OR)
decision_hinge: A union merges the node sets from several selector expressions; every resource that matches any of those expressions is selected. With unions, you can pass multiple arguments separated by spaces.

plausible_options.B: what the plain space between `state:modified+` and `result:error+` actually means for how these two selector expressions combine

eliminated_by.C: what the plain space between `state:modified+` and `result:error+` actually means
eliminated_by.D: what the plain space between `state:modified+` and `result:error+` actually means

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — an intersection is written with a comma and no space, the opposite of this syntax
distractor_traps.C: T1: fabricated — dbt's selection syntax defines no comma-free exclusion operator
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — both expressions are resolved and combined into one set for a single invocation, not run as sequential steps

stem: A reviewer needs the precise, documented scope of the `state:modified.configs` selector: which kinds of changes it tracks, and which specific ones it explicitly excludes. What does `state:modified.configs` identify?

option_texts.A: Changes to any node config, excluding changes to `database`, `schema`, `alias`, `tags`, or `meta`
option_texts.B: Changes to a model's schema YAML descriptions compared to the previous state artifact
option_texts.C: Changes to the database or schema a node resolves into, regardless of any other config
option_texts.D: Changes to upstream macros, whether called directly or indirectly by another macro

drill_answer_short: state:modified.configs tracks config changes, excluding database/schema/alias/tags/meta
decision_hinge: state:modified.configs: Changes to any node configs, excluding database/schema/alias/tags/meta.

plausible_options.B: A reviewer needs the precise, documented scope of the `state:modified.configs` selector

eliminated_by.C: which kinds of changes it tracks, and which specific ones it explicitly excludes
eliminated_by.D: which kinds of changes it tracks, and which specific ones it explicitly excludes

distractor_traps.B: T3: confusable sibling — description changes are tracked by the separate .persisted_descriptions subselector, not .configs
distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — database and schema changes are tracked by .relation, and .configs explicitly excludes them
distractor_traps.D: T3: confusable sibling — upstream macro changes are tracked by the separate .macros subselector

stem: Your data team has an SLA that the `reviews` source must be no more than 1 hour old before a freshness check reports a warning. Complete the config: `freshness: { warn_after: { count: 1, period: ____ } }`
drill_answer_short: period: hour, paired with count: 1, sets a one-hour warn threshold
decision_hinge: warn_after: How old the most recent data can be before a freshness check reports a warning. Requires both count and period.

stem: What flag do you pass to `dbt build` to specify the filesystem path to a previous invocation's state artifacts, so selectors like `state:modified` have something to compare against? Complete the command: `dbt build --select state:modified ____ ./prod-artifacts`
drill_answer_short: --state points dbt at the directory containing the comparison manifest
decision_hinge: The state method is used to select nodes by comparing them against a previous version of the same project. The file path of the comparison manifest must be specified via the --state flag.

stem: Looking at a lineage graph, a CI job runs `dbt ls --select @mart_fullmoon_reviews`. The team needs to confirm exactly what the `@` operator selects here, compared to a plain `+mart_fullmoon_reviews`. Which TWO statements are correct?

option_texts.A: `@mart_fullmoon_reviews` lists every node reachable as mart_fullmoon_reviews itself, its descendants, and the ancestors of those descendants
option_texts.B: `@` is useful in CI so a model's descendants can build successfully even if some of their other ancestors do not yet exist in the schema
option_texts.C: `@mart_fullmoon_reviews` and `+mart_fullmoon_reviews` always select exactly the same set of nodes
option_texts.D: `@` can only be placed after a model name, the same position where a trailing `+` goes

drill_answer_short: @ selects a node, its descendants, and the ancestors of those descendants, useful for CI
decision_hinge: The @ operator is similar to +, but will also include all ancestors of all descendants of the selected model. This is useful in continuous integration environments where you want to build a model and all of its descendants, but the ancestors of those descendants might not exist in the schema yet.

eliminated_by.D: The team needs to confirm exactly what the `@` operator selects here

distractor_traps.C: T3: confusable sibling — @ additionally pulls in ancestors of descendants, which a plain + does not, so the two sets can differ
distractor_traps.D: T1: fabricated — the @ operator is documented as placed at the front of the model name, not after it
